read.title: What a reference range means
text: A lab report prints each result next to a reference range. Laboratories usually build that range by testing many healthy people and keeping the middle 95 percent of their values. That simple fact has two consequences.

First, a value just outside the range is not automatically abnormal. By definition, about 1 healthy person in 20 falls outside the range for any single test, and when a panel reports 20 values at once, a healthy person will often have at least one flagged result. Second, a value inside the range does not guarantee health; it only means the number is common among healthy people.

Ranges also differ between laboratories because of different machines, methods and reference populations, and some depend on age, sex or altitude. Hemoglobin, for example, runs higher on average in adult males and in people living at high altitude. For this reason clinicians read a result against the range printed by the lab that ran it, look at trends over time, and interpret numbers together with the history and examination rather than in isolation.
